opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's a question I get a lot, and I think about it almost every day.

A startup shouldn't try to out-scale the big labs. If your strategy depends on having more compute, more data, or a bigger general-purpose model than OpenAI or DeepMind, you've already lost. They have resources we simply can't match. So the question becomes: where does focus beat scale?

For us, that answer is mathematics, and specifically formal, verifiable reasoning. The big labs are building generalist systems and have to care about a thousand use cases at once: coding, chat, search, enterprise, consumer. Math might be one benchmark on a long list for them. For us it's the whole company. That means we can make design choices a generalist lab wouldn't prioritize, like building deeply around formal languages such as Lean, where every proof can be checked by a machine. When your output is verifiable, you get a very clean signal for training and for trust, and you don't need the same brute-force scale to make progress.

The second thing is talent density. A small team where the mathematicians, the formal methods people, and the machine learning researchers sit together and argue every day can move very quickly. In a big organization those groups often sit far apart. In a startup the person who understands the theorem and the person who designs the training loop might be in the same conversation, and that shortens the iteration cycle a lot.

The third is speed and conviction. Large labs have to hedge. A startup can make a sharp bet and commit to it fully. If the bet is right, you can get to a frontier in a narrow domain before anyone else, and that domain can become a foundation for something much bigger. I think verified reasoning will matter far beyond math, in software verification, chip design, and anywhere correctness really matters.

Finally, I don't see it as purely competition. The big labs push the general capabilities forward, and that raises the floor for everyone, including us. Our job is to build the thing they aren't singularly focused on, and to be the best in the world at it.

r001.rationale: The response says a small startup can bring mathematicians, formal methods experts, and ML researchers together to shorten iteration, and can prioritize work generalist labs may not.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names talent density as an advantage and contrasts a closely integrated startup team with groups that may be separated in a large organization.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that OpenAI was once an underdog against Google.

r004.rationale: It advocates making a focused bet, but does not express belief in a competitive path despite being unable to prove that path exists.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I get asked this a lot, and my honest answer is that you don't compete with them head-on. If you try to build a slightly better general-purpose model with a fraction of their compute, you lose. That game is decided by scale, and scale is decided by capital.

So the question becomes where the big labs are structurally weak, not where they're strong. For us at Axiom, that's mathematics. A frontier lab treats math as one benchmark among fifty. They want to move the needle on a math eval, ship it, and move on to coding or agents or whatever the next priority is. We treat mathematics as the entire product. Every design decision, every piece of data, every evaluation is built around the question of whether the system can actually discover and verify new mathematical truth.

That focus gives you a few real advantages. First, you get to go deep where they go wide. Formal verification, for example, is a niche that requires understanding Lean, proof assistants, the actual culture of how mathematicians work. That's hard to prioritize inside an organization that has to serve a hundred million consumer users. Second, talent. The best mathematicians in the world don't necessarily want to be one of three thousand researchers at a big lab. They want to work on the problem they care about with people who understand it. A startup can offer that. Third, speed. We can change direction in a week. A large lab has a roadmap that's been negotiated across teams.

The other thing I'd say is that the ecosystem is actually becoming more favorable, not less. Open-weight models have gotten remarkably good, and compute, while expensive, is accessible in a way it wasn't three years ago. You don't need to pretrain from scratch to do meaningful frontier work in a vertical. You need the right data, the right training signal, and a very clear definition of what "good" means in your domain. In math, that definition is unusually crisp: a proof is either correct or it isn't. That's an enormous gift for a small team.

So my framing is that the big labs are building general intelligence, and we're trying to build a mathematician. Those are different problems, and I think the second one is winnable by a focused team.

r001.rationale: The response says a startup can focus on mathematics and formal verification in ways that are harder to prioritize at a large lab, and can offer mathematicians a chance to work on the problem they care about.

r002.rationale: It says a startup can attract mathematicians who may not want to work at a large lab, but does not identify talent density as a competitive dimension or acknowledge that larger labs have more talent overall.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention OpenAI having once been an underdog against Google.

r004.rationale: It says a focused team can win in mathematics, but does not advocate believing in a competitive path despite being unable to prove that the path exists.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to be very specific about where you can win. If you define the goal as building a better general-purpose model than the large labs, that’s a very expensive place to start. But having the strongest model doesn’t automatically mean having the best product for a particular customer.

An early-stage startup can choose a problem where it understands the user deeply, build something useful, and learn from actual use much faster. Maybe the hard part is fitting into an existing workflow, making the output reliable enough to act on, or figuring out what success should even look like. Those are opportunities for a small team to develop an advantage.

I’d also ask: as the underlying models get better, does our product become more valuable? You want those improvements to help you serve customers better, while your own advantage comes from the relationships, expertise, and feedback you accumulate. Start with a narrow problem that matters, solve it exceptionally well, and earn the right to expand.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fitting into a customer’s workflow, but does not identify supporting work that would be harder in another organizational environment as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It does not mention talent density as a way to compete with larger labs.

r003.rationale: It does not point out that OpenAI was once an underdog against Google.

r004.rationale: It recommends finding a narrow problem and building an advantage, but does not advocate believing a competitive path exists without proof.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to choose carefully where you compete. If you’re trying to build exactly what a large lab is building, and your only advantage is that you’ll work harder, that’s a difficult position. They have enormous resources and very talented people.

But a startup can focus on a problem that isn’t yet a priority for them. You can get very close to a particular group of users, understand where existing models fall short, and iterate quickly. Sometimes the advantage comes from better technology; sometimes it comes from how you integrate that technology into a workflow and make it reliable enough that people actually use it.

The question I would keep asking is: if the underlying models get much better next year, does that make our product more valuable, or does it eliminate the reason we exist? Ideally, you’re building something that benefits from that progress while developing your own strengths—whether that’s expertise, customer relationships, or a technical insight that others haven’t pursued.

r001.rationale: The response cites focus, user closeness, and fast iteration as advantages, but does not identify supporting work that would be harder in another organizational environment.

r002.rationale: It says large labs have talented people, but does not identify talent density as a dimension where a startup can compete.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention OpenAI having once been an underdog against Google.

r004.rationale: The response encourages finding a strategic path, but does not advocate believing a path exists without being able to prove it.
